topic.name: Computing Partial Derivatives Using the Rules of Differentiation

question.text: For the function $f(x,y) = x^3y^2+e^{xy},$ evaluate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ at the point $(-1,1).$
question.explanation:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

First, we use the sum rule for differentiation:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \big(x^3y^2+e^{xy}\big) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \big(x^3y^2\big) + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \big(e^{xy}\big) \end{align*}

Now, we use the chain rule and constant multiple rules for differentiation:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &=\dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \big(x^3y^2\big) + e^{xy} \cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} (xy) \\[5pt] &= y^2 \cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x}(x^3) + e^{xy} \cdot y\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \big(x \big) \\[5pt] &= y^2 \cdot 3x^2 + e^{xy} \cdot y\cdot 1 \\[5pt] &= 3x^2y^2 + ye^{xy} \end{align*} Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(-1,1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x}\Bigg|_{(-1,1)} &=3(-1)^2(1)^2+(1)e^{(-1)(1)} \\[5pt] &= 3+e^{-1} \end{align*}

question.text: For the function $f(x,y) = \sqrt{x+y} +x^2\sqrt{y},$ evaluate $f_y(3,1).$
question.explanation:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

First, we use the sum rule:

\begin{align} f_y(x,y) & = \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}\Big(\sqrt{x+y} +x^2\sqrt{y}\Big) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}\left(\sqrt{x+y}\right)+\dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}\left(x^2\sqrt{y}\right) \end{align}

Now, we use the chain and constant multiple rules:

\begin{align} \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}\left(\sqrt{x+y}\right)+\dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}\left(x^2\sqrt{y}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}} \cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}\left(x+y\right) + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}\left(x^2\sqrt{y}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}} \cdot \left(x\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}(1) + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}(y)\right) + x^2 \cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}\left(\sqrt{y}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}\cdot (0+1) +x^2 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}} + \dfrac{x^2}{2\sqrt{y}} \end{align}

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(3,1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_y(3,1) & = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3+1}} + \dfrac{3^2}{2\sqrt{1}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{9}{2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{19}{4} \end{align*}

question.text: Find $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ for $f(x,y) = (x+1)^{y^2}.$
question.explanation:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

First, we use the chain rule:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x}\left((x+1)^{y^2}\right) \\[5pt] & = y^2(x+1)^{y^2-1} \cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x}\left( x+1\right) \end{align*}

Now, we use the sum rule for differentiation:

\begin{align*} y^2(x+1)^{y^2-1} \cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x}\left( x+1\right) & = y^2(x+1)^{y^2-1} \cdot \left(\dfrac {\partial}{\partial x}\left( x \right) + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x}(1)\right) \\[5pt] &= y^2(x+1)^{y^2-1} \cdot (1 + 0) \\[5pt] &= y^2(x+1)^{y^2-1} \end{align*}

question.text: For the function $f(x,y) = \sqrt{x^2+y^2},$ evaluate $f_x\left(1,\sqrt{3}\right).$
question.explanation:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

First, we use the chain rule:

\begin{align} f_x(x,y) & = \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x}\Big(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\Big) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x}\left(x^2+y^2\right) \end{align}

Now, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differenciation:

\begin{align} \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x}\left(x^2+y^2\right) &= \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\cdot\left( \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x}\left(x^2\right) + y^2\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x}\left(1\right) \right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\cdot\left( 2x + y^2 \cdot 0 \right) \\[5pt] & =\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}} \end{align}

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $\left(1,\sqrt{3}\right)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_x\left(1,\sqrt{3}\right) & = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1^2 + (\sqrt{3})^2}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+3}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{align*}

question.text: Find $f_y(x,y)$ for $f(x,y) =\cos\left(\sqrt{2xy-1} \right).$
question.explanation:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

First, we use the chain rule:

\begin{align*} f_y(x,y) &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}\left(\cos\left(\sqrt{2xy-1} \right)\right) \\[5pt] &= -\sin\big(\sqrt{2xy-1}\big)\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}(\sqrt{2xy-1}) \\[5pt] &=-\sin\big(\sqrt{2xy-1}\big) \cdot \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2xy-1}}\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}(2xy-1) \end{align*}

Now, we use the sum and the constant multiple rules for differentiation:

\begin{align*} -\sin\big(\sqrt{2xy-1}\big) \cdot \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2xy-1}}\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}(2xy-1) &=-\dfrac{\sin\big(\sqrt{2xy-1}\big)}{2\sqrt{2xy-1}} \left( 2x\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}(y) -\dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}(1)\right) \\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{\sin\big(\sqrt{2xy-1}\big)}{2\sqrt{2xy-1}} \cdot (2x\cdot 1 - 0)\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{x\sin\big(\sqrt{2xy-1}\big)}{\sqrt{2xy-1}} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

question.text: For the function $f(x,y) =xy\cos{y}+ \sin{y},$ evaluate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ at the point $(2,\pi).$
question.explanation:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(xy\cos{y}+ \sin{y}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left( xy\cos{y} \right) - \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left( \sin{y}\right) \\[5pt] &= x\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(y\cos{y} \right)+ \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(\sin{y}\right) \end{align*}

Then, we use the product rule:

\begin{align*} x\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(y\cos{y} \right)+ \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(\sin{y}\right) &=x\left( \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}(y) \cdot \cos{y} + y \cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} (\cos{y}) \right) + \cos{y} \\[5pt] &= x\left( 1 \cdot \cos{y} + y \cdot (-\sin{y})\right) + \cos{y} \\[5pt] &=x\left( \cos{y}- y\sin{y} \right) + \cos{y} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(2,\pi)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y}\Bigg|_{(2,\pi)} & = 2\cdot \left( \cos{\pi}- \pi\cdot \sin{\pi} \right) + \cos{\pi} \\[5pt] & = 2(-1 - \pi\cdot 0) + (-1) \\[5pt] &= -3 \end{align*}

question.text: For the function $f(x,y) =ye^{xy}- x^2y^2,$ evaluate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ at the point $(1,1).$
question.explanation:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(ye^{xy}- x^2y^2\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left( ye^{xy} \right) - \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left( x^2y^2 \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left( ye^{xy} \right) - x^2\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(y^2 \right) \end{align*}

Then, we use the product, the chain, and the constant multiple rules:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left( ye^{xy} \right) - x^2\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(y^2 \right) &= \left( \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}(y) \cdot e^{xy} + y \cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} (e^{xy}) \right)- x^2\cdot (2y) \\[5pt] &= \left( 1 \cdot e^{xy} + y \cdot e^{xy}\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}(xy) \right)- 2x^2y \\[5pt] &=\left( e^{xy} + y\cdot e^{xy}\cdot x\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}(y) \right) - 2x^2y \\[5pt] &=\left( e^{xy} + y\cdot e^{xy}\cdot x\cdot 1 \right) - 2x^2y \\[5pt] &= e^{xy} + xye^{xy} - 2x^2y \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y}\Bigg|_{(1,1)} & = e^{1\cdot 1} + 1\cdot 1\cdot e^{1\cdot 1} - 2\cdot 1^2\cdot 1 \\[5pt] & = e + e - 2 \\[5pt] &= 2e-2 \end{align*}

question.text: Find $f_x(x,y)$ for $f(x,y) =x^3\cos(xy).$
question.explanation:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

First, we use the product rule:

\begin{align*} f_x(x,y) &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left( x^3\cos(xy) \right) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left( x^3\right)\cdot \cos(xy)+ x^3\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x}(\cos(xy)) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Then, we use the chain and constant multiple rules:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left( x^3\right)\cdot \cos(xy)+ x^3\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x}(\cos(xy)) &= (3x^2)\cdot \cos(xy)+ x^3\cdot (- \sin(xy)) \cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x}(xy) \\[5pt] &=3x^2\cos(xy)- x^3\sin(xy)\cdot y\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x}(x)\\[5pt] &= 3x^2\cos(xy)- x^3y\sin(xy)\cdot (1)\\[5pt] &= 3x^2\cos(xy) - x^3y\sin(xy) \end{align*}

question.text: Find $f_y(x,y)$ for $f(x,y) =xy\tan(y^2).$
question.explanation:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

First, we use the constant multiple rule and the product rule:

\begin{align*} f_y(x,y) &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(xy\tan(y^2)\right) \\[5pt] &=x \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left( y\tan(y^2)\right) \\[5pt] &= x\left(\dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}(y)\cdot \tan(y^2) + y\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}\left(\tan(y^2)\right)\right) \\[5pt] &= x \left((1)\cdot \tan(y^2) + y\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}\left(\tan(y^2)\right) \right) \\[5pt] &= x \tan(y^2) + xy\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}\left(\tan(y^2)\right) \end{align*}

Then, we use the chain rule:

\begin{align*} x \tan(y^2) + xy\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}\left(\tan(y^2)\right) &= x \tan(y^2) + xy\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}(\tan(y^2)) \\[5pt] &= x \tan(y^2) + xy\cdot \sec^2(y^2)\dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}(y^2) \\[5pt] &=x \tan(y^2) +xy\sec^2(y^2)\cdot (2y)\\[5pt] &= x \tan(y^2) + 2xy^2\sec^2(y^2) \end{align*}

question.text: Find $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ for $f(x,y) = x^4\cos{x} - xy^3.$
question.explanation:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left( x^4\cos{x} - xy^3 \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left( x^4\cos{x} \right) - \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left( xy^3 \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left( x^4\cos{x} \right) - y^3\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(x\right) \end{align*}

Then, we use the product rule:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left( x^4\cos{x} \right) - y^3\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(x\right) &=\left(\dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} (x^4)\cdot \cos{x} + x^4\cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} (\cos{x}) \right) - y^3 \cdot (1)\\[5pt] &= \left((4x^3) \cdot \cos{x} + x^4\cdot (-\sin{x})\right) - y^3 \\[5pt] &=4x^3\cos{x} - x^4\sin{x} - y^3 \end{align*}

question.text: Consider the function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{\tan(x-y)}{e^{x+y}}.$ The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ is given by \[ \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}} = \dfrac{h(x,y)}{e^{x+y}}. \] Find the function $h(x,y).$
question.explanation:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Using the quotient and chain rules, we have

\begin{align} \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \left( \dfrac{\tan(x-y)}{e^{x+y}} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (\tan(x-y)) \cdot e^{x+y} - \tan(x-y) \cdot \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (e^{x+y})}{\left(e^{x+y}\right)^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\sec^2(x-y)\cdot \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(x-y) \cdot e^{x+y} - \tan(x-y) \cdot e^{x+y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(x+y)}{\left(e^{x+y}\right)^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\sec^2(x-y)\cdot 1 \cdot e^{x+y} - \tan(x-y) \cdot e^{x+y}\cdot 1}{\left(e^{x+y}\right)^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\left(\sec^2(x-y) - \tan(x-y)\right)e^{x+y}}{\left(e^{x+y}\right)^2}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\sec^2(x-y) - \tan(x-y)}{e^{x+y}}. \end{align}

Therefore, we conclude that \[ h(x,y) = \sec^2(x-y) - \tan(x-y). \]

question.text: For the function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{\cos{x} + \sin{y}}{\cos{x} - \sin{y}},$ evaluate $\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}}$ at the point $\left(\pi, -\pi\right).$
question.explanation:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

First, we use the quotient rule: \begin{align} \dfrac{\partial}{\partial{y}} \left( \dfrac{\cos{x} + \sin{y}}{\cos{x} - \sin{y}} \right) &= \dfrac{\dfrac {\partial}{\partial{y}} (\cos{x} + \sin{y}) \cdot (\cos{x} - \sin{y}) - (\cos{x} + \sin{y}) \cdot \dfrac{\partial}{\partial{y}} (\cos{x} - \sin{y})}{(\cos{x} - \sin{y})^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\cos{y} \cdot (\cos{x} - \sin{y}) - (\cos{x} + \sin{y}) \cdot (-\cos{y})}{(\cos{x} - \sin{y})^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\cos{y}\cos{x} - \cos{y}\sin{y} + \cos{x}\cos{y} + \sin{y}\cos{y}}{(\cos{x} - \sin{y})^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2\cos{x}\cos{y}}{(\cos{x} - \sin{y})^2} \end{align}

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $\left(\pi, -\pi\right)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x}\Bigg|_{(\pi,-\pi)} & = \dfrac{2\cos{\pi}\cos(-\pi)}{(\cos{\pi} - \sin(-\pi))^2}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2(-1)(-1)}{(-1 - 0)^2}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2}{1}\\[5pt] & = 2 \end{align*}

question.text: For the function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{x+y}{\sin{y}},$ evaluate $\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}}$ at the point $\left(\pi,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right).$
question.explanation:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

First, we use the quotient rule: \begin{align} \dfrac{\partial}{\partial{y}} \left( \dfrac{x+y}{\sin{y}} \right) &= \dfrac{\dfrac {\partial}{\partial{y}} (x+y) \cdot \sin{y} - (x+y) \cdot \dfrac{\partial}{\partial{y}} (\sin{y})}{\sin^2{y}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1 \cdot \sin{y} - (x+y) \cdot \cos{y}}{\sin^2{y}} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\sin{y} - (x+y)\cos{y}}{\sin^2{y}} \end{align}

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $\left(\pi,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\Bigg|_{(\pi,\pi/2)} & = \dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) - \left(\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)}{\sin^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1 - 0}{1^2}\\[5pt] & = 1 \end{align*}

question.text: Consider the function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{3y - 2x}{7y - 6x}.$ The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ is given by \[ \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}} = \dfrac{h(x,y)}{(7y - 6x)^2}. \] Find the function $h(x,y).$
question.explanation:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Using the quotient rule, we have

\begin{align} \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \left( \dfrac{3y - 2x}{7y - 6x} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (3y-2x) \cdot (7y-6x) - (3y-2x) \cdot \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (7y-6x)}{(7y-6x)^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{(-2) \cdot (7y-6x) - (3y-2x) \cdot (-6)}{(7y-6x)^2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{-14y + 12x + 18y - 12x}{(7y-6x)^2}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{4y}{(7y-6x)^2} \end{align}

Therefore, we conclude that \[ h(x,y) = 4y. \]

question.text: For the function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2 - y^2}{e^{y-x}},$ evaluate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ at the point $(1,-1).$
question.explanation:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

First, we use the quotient and chain rules: \begin{align} \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \left( \dfrac{x^2 - y^2}{e^{y-x}} \right) & = \dfrac{\dfrac{\partial}{\partial{x}} (x^2 - y^2) \cdot e^{y-x} - (x^2 - y^2) \cdot \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (e^{y-x})}{\left(e^{y-x}\right)^2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2x \cdot e^{y-x} - (x^2 - y^2) \cdot e^{y-x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (y-x)}{\left(e^{y-x}\right)^2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2x e^{y-x} - (x^2 - y^2) \cdot e^{y-x}\cdot(-1)}{\left(e^{y-x}\right)^2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\left(2x + x^2 - y^2\right)e^{y-x}}{\left(e^{y-x}\right)^2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2x + x^2 - y^2}{e^{y-x}} \end{align}

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,-1)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\Bigg|_{(1,-1)} & = \dfrac{2(1) + 1^2 - (-1)^2}{e^{-1-1}}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2 + 1 - 1}{e^{-2}}\\[5pt] & = 2e^{2} \end{align*}

question.text: Find $f_{y}(x,y,z)$ for $f(x,y,z) = y^x - yz^3.$
question.explanation:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Using the sum and constant multiple rules, we have \begin{align} f_{y}(x,y,z) &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}\left( y^x - yz^3\right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}\left( y^x\right) -\dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(yz^3\right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}\left( y^x\right) - z^3 \cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} (y) \\[5pt] & = xy^{x-1} - z^3\cdot (1)\\[5pt] & = xy^{x-1}-z^3. \end{align}

question.text: Find $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}$ for $f(x,y,z) = e^{4y − xz^4}.$
question.explanation:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $z,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Using the chain rule, we have \begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial z} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z}\left(e^{4y − xz^4}\right) \\[5pt] & = e^{4y − xz^4} \cdot \dfrac{\partial}{\partial z} \left(4y − xz^4\right) \end{align*}

Then, we use the sum and constant multiple rules: \begin{align} e^{4y − xz^4} \cdot \dfrac{\partial}{\partial z} \left(4y − xz^4\right) & = e^{4y − xz^4} \cdot \left( \dfrac{\partial}{\partial z} (4y) − \dfrac{\partial}{\partial z}\left(xz^4\right) \right) \\[5pt] & = e^{4y − xz^4} \cdot \left(0 - x\dfrac{\partial}{\partial z} \left(z^4\right) \right)\\[5pt] & = -e^{4y − xz^4} \cdot x \cdot 4z^3\\[5pt] & = -4xz^3e^{4y − xz^4} \end{align}

Therefore, \[ \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} = -4xz^3e^{4y − xz^4}. \]

question.text: For the function $f(x,y,z) = x^2y^2-\ln (xz),$ evaluate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ at the point $(1,0,1).$
question.explanation:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \big(x^2y^2-\ln (xz)\big) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \big(x^2y^2\big) - \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \big(\ln (xz)\big) \\[5pt] &= x^2 \cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}(y^2) - (0) \\[5pt] &=x^2 \cdot (2y) \\[5pt] &= 2x^2y \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,0,1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y}\Bigg|_{(1,0,1)} &=2(1)^2(0) \\[5pt] &= 0 \end{align*}

question.text: For the function $f(x,y,z) = xz^3-x^2\cos (\pi y),$ evaluate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ at the point $(1,1,2).$
question.explanation:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules: \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left( xz^3-x^2\cos (\pi y)\right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\partial }{\partial x}\left(xz^{3}\right) - \dfrac{\partial }{\partial x}(x^2\cos(\pi y))\\[5pt] &= z^3 \cdot \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \left( x \right) - \cos (\pi y) \cdot \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left( x^2\right) \\[5pt] &= z^3 \cdot 1 - \cos (\pi y) \cdot 2x \\[5pt] &= z^3 -2x\cos (\pi y) \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,1,2)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\Bigg|_{(1,1,2)} & = 2^3 - 2(1)\cos(\pi(1))\\[5pt] & = 8 - 2(1)(-1)\\[5pt] & = 8 + 2\\[5pt] & = 10 \end{align*}

question.text: For the function $f(x,y,z) = z^2e^{xy}-y^2e^{yz},$ evaluate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}$ at the point $(0,-1,1).$
question.explanation:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $z,$ treating all other variables as constants.

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules: \begin{align} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial z} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial z} \left( z^2e^{xy}-y^2e^{yz}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial z} \left( z^2e^{xy}\right)-\dfrac{\partial}{\partial z} \left(y^2e^{yz}\right) \\[5pt] &=e^{xy}\cdot \dfrac{\partial}{\partial z} \left( z^2\right) -y^2\cdot\dfrac{\partial}{\partial z} \left(e^{yz}\right) \\[5pt] \end{align}

Then, we use the chain rule: \begin{align} e^{xy}\cdot \dfrac{\partial}{\partial z} \left( z^2\right) -y^2 \cdot \dfrac{\partial}{\partial z} \left(e^{yz}\right) & = e^{xy}\cdot 2z -y^2 \cdot e^{yz} \cdot \dfrac{\partial}{\partial z} \left(yz\right) \\[5pt] &= e^{xy}\cdot 2z-y^2\cdot e^{yz}\cdot y\\[5pt] &=2ze^{xy}-y^3e^{yz} \end{align}

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(0,-1,1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial z}\Bigg|_{(0,-1,1)} & = 2(1)e^{(0)(-1)}-(-1)^3e^{(-1)(1)}\\[5pt] & =2+e^{-1} \end{align*}
